$1=a$, $2=b$, $3=n$. For each site $n$ this gives
$$R_{ab}(u-v)R_{an}(u)R_{bn}(v) =R_{bn}(v)R_{an}(u)R_{ab}(u-v).$$
This identity acts on $V_a\otimes V_b\otimes V_n$ and as the identity on
every other site.

Write $R_{ab}=R_{ab}(u-v)$, $R_{an}=R_{an}(u)$ and
$R_{bn}=R_{bn}(v)$. For $1\le n\le N$ set
$T_a^{(n)}(u):=R_{an}(u)\cdots R_{a1}(u)$ and
$T_b^{(n)}(v):=R_{bn}(v)\cdots R_{b1}(v)$. The case $n=1$ of the desired
identity is step 1.1. Suppose it holds for $n-1$. Operators
$T_a^{(n-1)}$ commute with $R_{bn}(v)$, and $R_{an}(u)$ commutes with
$T_b^{(n-1)}$, because their auxiliary and physical tensor factors are
disjoint. Therefore
$$\begin{aligned} R_{ab}T_a^{(n)}T_b^{(n)} &=R_{ab}R_{an}R_{bn}T_a^{(n-1)}T_b^{(n-1)}\\ &=R_{bn}R_{an}R_{ab}T_a^{(n-1)}T_b^{(n-1)}\\ &=R_{bn}R_{an}T_b^{(n-1)}T_a^{(n-1)}R_{ab}\\ &=T_b^{(n)}T_a^{(n)}R_{ab}, \end{aligned}$$
where the second equality is step 1.1 at site $n$, the third is the induction
hypothesis, and the final equality uses the other disjoint-site commutation.
The argument holds for each $n$ up to $N$, proving the claimed RTT identity.

Taking $n=N$ in step 2.1 gives the stated monodromy relation with
$T_a^{(N)}=T_a$ and $T_b^{(N)}=T_b$. No invertibility assumption on
$R_{ab}(u-v)$ is used, so the identity also holds at its singular spectral
differences.

derivations.claim:
At $u=0$, every factor is $R_{aj}(0)=iP_{aj}$, so
$t(0)=i^N\operatorname{tr}_a(P_{aN}\cdots P_{a1})$. On an elementary chain
tensor $e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_N}$, start the auxiliary factor at
each basis vector $e_a$ in turn. The swaps pass $e_{j_1},\ldots,e_{j_N}$
successively to the auxiliary factor and shift the preceding entries one site
right; the auxiliary trace retains exactly the term with $e_a=e_{j_N}$. The
output is therefore $e_{j_N}\otimes e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{N-1}}$.
These tensors form a basis, hence $\operatorname{tr}_a(P_{aN}\cdots P_{a1})=U$.
As $U$ permutes a basis, it is invertible, proving the first identity and
invertibility of $t(0)$.

Differentiate the finite product defining $T_a(u)$ and use
$R'_{aj}(0)=I_{aj}$. For each $m$, let
$D_m=\operatorname{tr}_a(P_{aN}\cdots P_{a,m+1}P_{a,m-1}\cdots P_{a1})$,
with the factor $P_{am}$ omitted. Following the auxiliary basis vector
through the remaining swaps and taking its trace gives, for $2\le m<N$,
$$D_m(e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_N})= e_{j_N}\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{r=1}^{m-2}e_{j_r}\right)\otimes e_{j_m}\otimes e_{j_{m-1}}\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{r=m+1}^{N-1}e_{j_r}\right).$$
An empty tensor block in this display is omitted.
For $m=N$ the same calculation gives
$e_{j_{N-1}}\otimes e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{N-2}}\otimes e_{j_N}$;
for $m=1$ it gives
$e_{j_1}\otimes e_{j_N}\otimes e_{j_2}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{N-1}}$.
In each case this is exactly $UP_{m-1,m}$ applied to the input, with
$P_{0,1}:=P_{N,1}$. Since the elementary tensors form a basis,
$D_m=UP_{m-1,m}$ as operators. Thus
$t'(0)=i^{N-1}\sum_{m=1}^N UP_{m-1,m}$.

From step 1.1, $t(0)^{-1}=i^{-N}U^{-1}$. The definition of $U$ shows
$UP_{m-1,m}U^{-1}=P_{m,m+1}$ for $2\le m\le N$, while
$UP_{N,1}U^{-1}=P_{1,2}$. Therefore
$t'(0)t(0)^{-1}=i^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^N P_{m,m+1}=-i\sum_{m=1}^N P_{m,m+1}$.
Multiplication by $i$ proves the claimed logarithmic-derivative identity.

dimensionless complex parameter $u$.

For the ordered periodic monodromies
$$T_a(u):=R_{aN}(u)\cdots R_{a1}(u),\qquad T_b(v):=R_{bN}(v)\cdots R_{b1}(v),$$
the finite-dimensional operator identity
$$R_{ab}(u-v)T_a(u)T_b(v)=T_b(v)T_a(u)R_{ab}(u-v)$$
holds on $V_a\otimes V_b\otimes V_N$ for every $u,v\in\mathbb C$.

derivations.claim:
Put $s=u-v$. Since $P_{ab}^2=I$ and the mixed terms cancel,
$R_{ab}(s)R_{ab}(-s)=-(s^2+1)I$; hence $R_{ab}(s)$ is invertible for
$s\ne i,-i$. By [F3],
$T_b(v)T_a(u)=R_{ab}(s)T_a(u)T_b(v)R_{ab}(s)^{-1}$. The factor $R_{ab}$
acts only on the finite auxiliary space $V_a\otimes V_b$, so the ordinary
finite trace over that space is cyclic even with operator-valued coefficients
on $V_N$. Also $\operatorname{tr}_{ab}(T_a(u)T_b(v))=t(u)t(v)$ and
$\operatorname{tr}_{ab}(T_b(v)T_a(u))=t(v)t(u)$, by expanding each auxiliary
matrix in matrix units. Taking $\operatorname{tr}_{ab}$ therefore proves
$[t(u),t(v)]=0$ whenever $u-v\ne\pm i$.

Each entry of $t(u)$ is a polynomial in $u$, because it is the trace of a
finite product of matrices whose entries are linear polynomials. Thus every
entry of $[t(u),t(v)]$ is a polynomial in $(u,v)$. For each fixed $v$, it
vanishes for every $u$ except at most $v+i$ and $v-i$; a one-variable
polynomial with infinitely many zeros is zero. This holds for every $v$, so
$[t(u),t(v)]=0$ for all complex $u,v$, including the two singular
differences.

By [F2], $t(0)$ is invertible; hence $M(u)=t(0)^{-1}t(u)$ is analytic near
$0$ and $M(0)=I$. Choose a submultiplicative matrix norm. Continuity of $M$
gives a neighborhood of $0$ where $\|M(u)-I\|<1$, and there define
$\log M(u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}(M(u)-I)^n/n$, a convergent matrix power
series. Step 2.1 implies $t(u)$ commutes with $t(w)$ and every $t(v)$; since
$t(0)$ is invertible, $t(0)^{-1}$ commutes with them as well. Thus $M(u)$,
$M(w)$, and each $t(v)$ commute. Their logarithmic power series preserve
these commutations. Comparing the convergent two-variable Taylor coefficients
proves the coefficient matrices commute pairwise and with every $t(v)$.

Fix an integer $N\ge3$. Let $V=\mathbb C^2$ with ordered basis
$e_\uparrow,e_\downarrow$, let $V_N=V^{\otimes N}$ in left-to-right site
order, and let $V_a=V$ be an auxiliary copy. For $u\in\mathbb C$, define
$R_{aj}(u)=uI_{aj}+iP_{aj}$ on $V_a\otimes V_N$, where $P_{aj}$ swaps the
auxiliary factor and site $j$. Define
$$T_a(u)=R_{aN}(u)\cdots R_{a1}(u),\qquad t(u)=\operatorname{tr}_a T_a(u),$$
where products mean composition with the rightmost factor acting first, and
$\operatorname{tr}_a$ is the ordinary finite-dimensional trace over $V_a$.
For distinct sites $j,k$, $P_{jk}$ swaps those two tensor factors. Define the
oriented cyclic shift by
$$U(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N)=v_N\otimes v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{N-1}.$$
The spectral parameter $u$ is dimensionless. All operators in this definition
are finite-dimensional complex-linear endomorphisms.

For the ordered monodromy on $V_N$ with $V=\mathbb C^2$, define the shifted
site operator $L_{aj}(u):=R_{aj}(u-i/2)$, shifted monodromy
$T_a^L(u):=L_{aN}(u)\cdots L_{a1}(u)$, and shifted transfer matrix
$\tau(u):=\operatorname{tr}_aT_a^L(u)$. In the ordered auxiliary basis
$e_\uparrow,e_\downarrow$, write
$$T_a^L(u)=\begin{pmatrix}A(u)&B(u)\\C(u)&D(u)\end{pmatrix}_a, \qquad \Omega:=e_\uparrow^{\otimes N}.$$
For an integer $M$ with $0\le M\le N$, a **regular on-shell Bethe datum** is
a tuple of finite complex numbers $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_M$ satisfying all
of the following conditions:

1. The roots are pairwise distinct, none equals $i/2$ or $-i/2$, and no
   difference $\lambda_j-\lambda_k$ for $j\ne k$ equals $i$ or $-i$.
2. For each $j=1,\ldots,M$,
   $$\left(\frac{\lambda_j+i/2}{\lambda_j-i/2}\right)^N =\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{\lambda_j-\lambda_k+i}{\lambda_j-\lambda_k-i}.$$
3. The associated vector
   $$\Psi(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_M):= B(\lambda_1)\cdots B(\lambda_M)\Omega$$
   is nonzero.

For $M=0$ the root tuple and products are empty and $\Psi=\Omega$. This
definition records regular solutions and nonzero vectors only; it makes no
claim of completeness, covers no singular-root regularization, and does not
include descendants generated from other reference vectors.

For the ordered periodic monodromies
$$T_a(u):=R_{aN}(u)\cdots R_{a1}(u),\qquad T_b(v):=R_{bN}(v)\cdots R_{b1}(v),$$
the finite-dimensional operator identity
$$R_{ab}(u-v)T_a(u)T_b(v)=T_b(v)T_a(u)R_{ab}(u-v)$$
holds on $V_a\otimes V_b\otimes V_N$ for every $u,v\in\mathbb C$.

derivations.claim:
Apply [F3] at $x=u-i/2$ and $y=v-i/2$. Since the two shifts cancel in
$x-y$, the shifted monodromies obey
$$R_{ab}(u-v)T_a^L(u)T_b^L(v)=T_b^L(v)T_a^L(u)R_{ab}(u-v).$$
All operators act on finite-dimensional auxiliary and chain tensor factors.

On a single site with the site vector $e_\uparrow$, direct application of
$L_{aj}(u)=(u-i/2)I+iP_{aj}$ gives the auxiliary matrix
$$L_{aj}(u)e_\uparrow= \begin{pmatrix}(u+i/2)e_\uparrow&i e_\downarrow\\ 0&(u-i/2)e_\uparrow\end{pmatrix}_a.$$
It is upper triangular; multiplying these local matrices in the prescribed
site order keeps the product upper triangular on
$\Omega=e_\uparrow^{\otimes N}$. Its diagonal entries multiply, so
$$C(u)\Omega=0,\qquad A(u)\Omega=a(u)\Omega,\qquad D(u)\Omega=d(u)\Omega, \quad a(u)=(u+i/2)^N,\quad d(u)=(u-i/2)^N.$$

In the ordered auxiliary basis
$|\uparrow\uparrow\rangle,|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle,
|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\downarrow\rangle$,
$R_{ab}(x)$ has diagonal entries $x+i,x,x,x+i$ and the two off-diagonal
middle entries $i$. Comparing the row $|\uparrow\uparrow\rangle$ and column
$|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle$ entries in step 1.1 gives
$$(x+i)B(u)A(v)=iB(v)A(u)+xA(v)B(u),\qquad x=u-v.$$
Exchange $u,v$ and solve for $A(u)B(v)$ to obtain
$A(u)B(v)=f(x)B(v)A(u)+g(x)B(u)A(v)$ for $x\ne0$, where
$f(x):=(x-i)/x$ and $g(x):=i/x$. The row $|\uparrow\uparrow\rangle$,
column $|\downarrow\downarrow\rangle$ entry gives
$(x+i)B(u)B(v)=(x+i)B(v)B(u)$, hence the $B$ operators commute for $x\ne-i$;
both sides are polynomial matrices, so this holds also at $x=-i$. The row
$|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle$, column $|\downarrow\downarrow\rangle$ entry
gives $xD(u)B(v)+iB(u)D(v)=(x+i)B(v)D(u)$. Thus for $x\ne0$,
$D(u)B(v)=h(x)B(v)D(u)+k(x)B(u)D(v)$, where
$h(x):=(x+i)/x$ and $k(x):=-i/x$.

For pairwise distinct parameters $v_1,\ldots,v_M$ and a variable $u$
distinct from them, the exchange relations of step 2.1 imply
$$\begin{aligned} A(u)\prod_{k=1}^M B(v_k)\Omega ={}&a(u)\prod_{k=1}^M f(u-v_k)\prod_{k=1}^M B(v_k)\Omega\\ &+\sum_{j=1}^M a(v_j)g(u-v_j) \prod_{k\ne j}f(v_j-v_k)\,B(u)\prod_{k\ne j}B(v_k)\Omega,\\ D(u)\prod_{k=1}^M B(v_k)\Omega ={}&d(u)\prod_{k=1}^M h(u-v_k)\prod_{k=1}^M B(v_k)\Omega\\ &+\sum_{j=1}^M d(v_j)k(u-v_j) \prod_{k\ne j}h(v_j-v_k)\,B(u)\prod_{k\ne j}B(v_k)\Omega. \end{aligned}$$
For $M=0$ these follow from step 1.2. Suppose they hold for $M-1$ and move
$A(u)$ past the first factor $B(v_1)$ using step 2.1, then apply the induction
formulas to the remaining $M-1$ factors. The unwanted coefficient for a fixed
$j\ge2$ is the common factor
$a(v_j)\prod_{k\ne1,j}f(v_j-v_k)$ times
$f(x)g(y)+g(x)g(y-x)$, with $x=u-v_1$ and $y=u-v_j$. Direct substitution
of $f(z)=(z-i)/z$ and $g(z)=i/z$ gives
$f(x)g(y)+g(x)g(y-x)=g(y)f(x-y)$; here $x-y=v_j-v_1$, the missing factor
in the target product. For $j=1$, the second term of the first exchange gives
the displayed coefficient directly. For $D$, the same induction uses
$h,k$ and the identity
$h(x)k(y)+k(x)k(y-x)=k(y)h(x-y)$, verified by substituting
$h(z)=(z+i)/z$ and $k(z)=-i/z$. This proves both formulas for all $M$.

Apply step 3.1 with $v_j=\lambda_j$ and add its $A$ and $D$ equations.
The coefficient of $\prod_kB(\lambda_k)\Omega$ is exactly $\Lambda(u)$ in
the statement. For each $j$, the combined coefficient of
$B(u)\prod_{k\ne j}B(\lambda_k)\Omega$ is
$$g(u-\lambda_j)\left[ a(\lambda_j)\prod_{k\ne j}f(\lambda_j-\lambda_k) -d(\lambda_j)\prod_{k\ne j}h(\lambda_j-\lambda_k) \right],$$
because $k(u-\lambda_j)=-g(u-\lambda_j)$. The bracket is zero: after
substituting $a,d,f,h$, its equality is precisely the Bethe equation in
[F2], whose denominators are nonzero by the regularity hypotheses. Thus
$\tau(u)\Psi=\Lambda(u)\Psi$ for every $u$ outside the finite root set.

Put $Q(u)=\prod_{j=1}^M(u-\lambda_j)$. The numerator of $\Lambda(u)$ is
$$P(u)=a(u)\prod_{j=1}^M(u-\lambda_j-i) +d(u)\prod_{j=1}^M(u-\lambda_j+i),$$
a polynomial. At $u=\lambda_j$, its value is
$$P(\lambda_j)=i\left[ d(\lambda_j)\prod_{k\ne j}(\lambda_j-\lambda_k+i) -a(\lambda_j)\prod_{k\ne j}(\lambda_j-\lambda_k-i) \right]=0$$
by the same Bethe equation. Since the $\lambda_j$ are distinct, each is a
simple root of $Q$, so the factor theorem gives $Q\mid P$ and $\Lambda=P/Q$
is a polynomial. Both $\tau(u)\Psi$ and $\Lambda(u)\Psi$ are then polynomial
vector-valued functions agreeing away from finitely many points by step 4.1;
their difference has infinitely many zeros and is identically zero. As
$\Psi\ne0$ by [F2], this is an eigenvector identity for every $u$, with no
claim that other eigenvectors arise this way.

Use the periodic convention $P_{N,N+1}:=P_{N,1}$. The rational transfer
matrix satisfies
$$i\,t'(0)t(0)^{-1}=\sum_{j=1}^N P_{j,j+1}.$$
Consequently, for real $J,c$, the finite matrix
$$H_N:=J\sum_{j=1}^N P_{j,j+1}+cI$$
is Hermitian and commutes with every $t(u)$. If $H_N$ is interpreted as a
physical energy in the stated QSM convention, $J$ and $c$ are in joules.
For the Pauli matrices
$$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},$$
the adjacent swap on $V\otimes V$ is
$$P=\frac{I+X\otimes X+Y\otimes Y+Z\otimes Z}{2}.$$

derivations.claim:
For a fixed $j$, exactly two of the $N$ periodic bonds touch site $j$;
they are distinct because $N\ge3$. Each of the other $N-2$ swaps exchanges
two up spins and fixes $|j\rangle$, while the two touching swaps move the down
spin to $j-1$ and $j+1$. Therefore
$$H_N|j\rangle=J\big((N-2)|j\rangle+|j-1\rangle+|j+1\rangle\big),$$
with indices interpreted modulo $N$.

The vectors $|j\rangle$ are linearly independent and every coefficient
$e^{ik_mj}$ has modulus one, so $|k_m\rangle\ne0$. Since
$e^{ik_mN}=1$, periodic reindexing gives
$\sum_j e^{ik_mj}|j-1\rangle=e^{ik_m}|k_m\rangle$ and
$\sum_j e^{ik_mj}|j+1\rangle=e^{-ik_m}|k_m\rangle$. Applying step 1.1
linearly now yields
$H_N|k_m\rangle=J(N-2+e^{ik_m}+e^{-ik_m})|k_m\rangle$; using
$e^{ik_m}+e^{-ik_m}=2\cos k_m$ proves the claimed eigenvalue.
